always: Name people the way their families in this world would have: from the language, class and era the setting implies. Use names real people carry or have carried; a name never announces who someone is. Each genre's examples show the kind of name, so choose others like them.

styles.names: Ordinary names of the setting's country and decade, the kind on a class list or a work rota: Lisa, Jonas, Emma Berg, Dave. Mostly common names, and nicknames the way friends use them.
Common, forgettable names of the setting's place and time, as a police report would list them: Karen Holt, Mehmet Aydin, Paul Lindqvist.
Plain names of the setting's place and time, so the dread lands on ordinary people: Jenny, Mark Doyle, Carol Webb.
Names of a 1940s American city, clipped by use, with the immigrant surnames of its neighbourhoods: Lou Barelli, Vera Novak, Frankie Doyle.
Period names of the setting's place and century, spelled as a parish register spells them: Agnes, Edmund Pole, Harriet, Josiah Crane.
Names of the rural American South, handed down and shortened: Lurleen, Boyd, Darla Pruitt, Earl Junior.
English names of the 1810s, gentry and servants alike, with the titles and forms of address of the day: Miss Harriet Lowe, Mr Bramley, Sukey, Tom.
Names of an old university's students and fellows in the setting's country, family names often used as first names: Hugo Lattimer, Margaret, Kit Avery.
Names of a court's nobility and household drawn from one real language and its titles: Countess Ilse von Brandt, Lord Osbert, Father Anselm, the steward Gerlach.
Names from one real old language the setting suggests, such as Old Norse, Welsh, Occitan, Czech or Persian, short and worn by use like medieval names: Hild, Osric, Berthe, Wat the cooper.
Old-fashioned rural names of the region the setting suggests, repeated down the generations: Hester, Amos, Ruth Pennick, old Mother Darrow.
Names in the language of the myth the setting draws on, attested or built the way that language builds them: Kleon or Ismene for Greek myth, Sigrun for Norse.
Chinese names in pinyin, family name first, with sect titles, courtesy names and nicknames: Zhao Wen, Elder Sister Lin, Old Man Qiu.
Names of the 1870s frontier, Anglo, Mexican, Chinese and Native alike, with nicknames earned: Josiah Pell, Mercy, Lupe Ortega, Two-Bit Cal.
Names of the 1930s for the expedition, and for the locals the names they give themselves: Dorothy Fenn, Max Adler, Rashid al-Tamimi.
Names real people carry today, mixed by migration and drifted a little by time: Ade Okafor, Ines Park, Tomasz, Yuki Brandt. Invent names for ships, not for people.
The real mix of languages of the city the setting suggests, and street handles that are ordinary words or nicknames: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz, Big Sergei, Dot.
Names real people of the region carry, with the odd newer word-name used sparingly: Femi, Johanna Ek, Luz, Tavi.
Names from before the collapse, worn down by use, and a few children named after what survivors value: Pete, Dee Marsh, Kowalski, a girl called Salt.
Plain period names of the setting's place, as on a deed or a death notice; the strangeness belongs to the things, not the people: Wilbur Hale, Edith Marsh.
